title: Fewer slides, more dragons
content:
Comments

hypfer · Nov 21, 2026

This to me feels more like a novelty that will wear out rather quickly than truly the way forward.

I suppose it will also exist, sometimes, but a simple ppt actually gets the job of a ppt done quite reliably and without pulling away attention from the actual content.

I think it is a wrong assumption that something needs to be colorful and flashy for people to want to engage with it. Unless people are toddlers that is.

Professional humans might be very engaged with black text on a white slide, provided that the text encodes an interesting problem, thought or topic.

bobbyraduloff · Nov 21, 2026

If my manager were to use this, I'd be genuinely concerned about the direction they're setting. It speaks to a lack of focus and inability to prioritize the important parts of a problem. I'd make me wonder what the decision making process was like for everything else and if things were picked because they're flashy and cool or because of their intrinsic value...

MDCore · Nov 21, 2026

Being a manager isn't pure strategy, delivery or (thank goodness) pure administrivia. Building fun things that encourage teamwork and make a potentially boring day more interesting or a dull presentation more engaging is valuable work. TFA even mentions how these things take a lot less time than before. Don't confuse flashy and cool with a lack of value, they are not mutually exclusive.

trescenzi · Nov 21, 2026

I’ll take the other side of this. We all need more whimsy in our lives. The work most people do isn’t a matter of life or death. Having fun makes work more enjoyable and helps you avoid burn out. I genuinely dislike working with people who are overly serious. They make the job less interesting and I worry about their ability to prioritize because if they find that spending 15min to have an AI make a presentation more entertaining and engaging a waste of time then they don’t understand their audience are humans and not robots. Life is short; (most) work isn’t that important; live a little.

zkmon · Nov 21, 2026

When you are trying to get clarity on your own thoughts or making plans for your next few weeks of travel etc, do you create slides to discuss it with yourself? It is most likely a text file with minimal, but very clear points. That's because you are the closest person to yourself, having full context. People around you are not complete strangers. They have varying level of context about what you are talking about.

If you have to spend so much on whether to have slides or not, or what should be in place of them, new AI strategies etc, there is fundamentally something wrong with your audience context.

Who is your audience? some strangers who have no context of what you are talking about? Some buyers with cash who want to be impressed by the colors, themes and animations in your slides?

For most of my work situations, it is neither. It is a handful of people who already have the full context and just need to align on a few things. So in most cases, my slides boil down to a text file with short lines.

In some social groups (or gangster movies), the boss doesn't even need to say words. Just the looks and gestures are enough to interpret the orders and align everyone into a single goal.

giladd · Nov 21, 2026

Comments here say that these colorful techniques for info presentation are not needed when your audience is professional and already knows the context of the discussed topic. While true, many organizations don't have that, certainly not for all members at all levels!

Sometimes taking a marketing approach for passing information or ideas is the right call. Not all colleges are engaged, knowledgeable or even decent enough to listen during the meeting. You still have to work with the cards you're dealt. Being flashy is one way to do it.

MDCore · Nov 21, 2026

Yes, the idea that presentation format is irrelevant is a silly one. No one is immune to "marketing", but if you are, great, the rest of your team or your stakeholders are not. Learning different ways to convey information and ideas to different audiences is a valuable leadership skill.

IrishTechie · Nov 21, 2026

I think far too many people think they can do this, so you end up on meetings where the presenter goes around in circles or dives down rabbit holes of uninteresting irrelevances. I’m not a huge fan of slides, but they do force the average person to put a bit of thought into what they’re going to say in advance.

gyomu · Nov 21, 2026

This just looks like cramming slides with bold words and 6 point text, but with extra steps?

Golden rule I've always followed is to stick to a single idea/image/video per slide; if you're showing complicated things (eg large data tables, graphs, etc.) give people access so they can look at it on their own screen.

If running through your deck takes more than 15-30 minutes (discussion included) you probably need to rethink whether it's the best medium.

Fun! But I would hesitate to draw conclusions from this, mostly due to the power imbalance. If an employee understands that the manager wants them to have fun, they will fake engagement.

Would be different if we saw the same signals when presenting up rather than down.

I guess try it out in a board meeting, maybe a colorful ball pit style walkthrough of OKRs?
